chapter: Studio recordings of the late twenties and thirties
title: Never out of work in the Depression
summary: Morehouse worked straight through the Depression; Hutto credits NBC and CBS staff work, the first Hit Parade broadcasts and his versatility on vibes.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: The Depression years and the WPA band

blocks.x: Uh huh, okay. This was during the Depression when a lot of musicians were out of work.
You didn't have the problem of a lot of musicians. You were working.
How did you manage to do, how did you manage to find so many jobs when there were so many musicians that couldn't find jobs?
You had no trouble finding work, did you?
I don't know. I don't know why.
There must have been other drummers but you had your fill of work.
Yeah. These singers, when they recorded, did they ask for you? Did they know you and want you?
Did you have any problems at all during the Depression?
You just worked right through it.
I think the ad said and we use it - never unemployed a day during the Depression, because of his work, I guess mainly at NBC studios.

And I guess later CBS also. And of course he was with Lennie Hayton as we said and also in the first Hit Parade broadcasts in 1935. And we have a cut of that, we have Chauncey's vibes in the background.
Can you account for the reason unlike so many other musicians, he was never unemployed for a day?

I don't know. I guess certain ones, I guess Goodman in the biography that sometimes Goodman's income might have gone down to $40 a week. But I guess the good ones, and Chauncey of course played the whole percussion instruments and he had taken vibraphone lessons and that gave him a little more versatility. Maybe then....
I guess Krupa was busy all the time. But I don't know that Gene played anything except drums.
